Key Message 1...Primarily dry weather is expected through Saturday.

A high pressure ridge at the surface and aloft builds and then
crests E'ward across Western and Central NY today so that by
sunset this evening, the surface ridge axis will become located
near Lake Champlain and Long Island. Stabilizing subsidence 
accompanying the ridge will promote fair weather. Considerably
clear sky, weak surface winds, and lingering low-level moisture
from recent rainfall will continue to allow patchy radiation fog
and river valley steam fog to develop through daybreak this
morning. Fog is then expected to dissipate by late morning,
following the onset of diurnal convective mixing of the boundary
layer. Daytime heating and the development of synoptic-scale
low-level warm air advection as our CWA becomes located along
the western flank of the surface ridge will allow highs to reach
mainly the upper 70's to mid 80's late this afternoon. The
coolest highs are expected in the higher terrain of the Western
Southern Tier, Finger Lakes, and Eastern Lake Ontario Region, as
well as along and very near the shores of ~74F Lake Erie and 
~73F Lake Ontario due to lake breeze development late this 
morning through early evening. 
 
Current odds favor fair weather persisting tonight through
Saturday as the aforementioned ridge exits very slowly E'ward
and a positively-tilted shortwave trough approaches from the 
western Great Lakes and vicinity. However, moist isentropic 
ascent aloft, ahead of the shortwave trough axis, may release 
sufficient elevated CAPE to generate very isolated showers and 
thunderstorms over western Lake Ontario and vicinity during the 
predawn hours of Saturday morning. Even so, the chance of this 
shower/storm development is only 20% at most. Overnight lows 
should reach mainly the mid 50's to mid 60's around daybreak 
Saturday and be followed by late afternoon highs reaching mainly
the 80's. Humidity will increase tonight and especially on 
Saturday as more-direct low-level warm/moist air advection from 
the Gulf and southern Gulf Stream becomes established. 

Key Message 2...Showers and thunderstorms develop for the second 
half of the weekend, bringing the potential for another round 
of heavy rainfall.

The above-mentioned shortwave trough axis should move from the
western Great Lakes to near western New England and NJ during 
Saturday night through Monday night. At the surface, the 
attendant cold front should approach our region from the 
northwest Saturday night through Sunday before drifting SE'ward 
across our CWA Sunday night through early Monday afternoon as 
multiple lows move NE'ward along the front. Behind the front and
shortwave trough axis, a high pressure ridge at the surface and
aloft should build slowly from the western Great Lakes and 
vicinity Sunday night through Monday night. Periods of scattered
to widespread showers and thunderstorms are expected Saturday 
night through Sunday night as weak to moderate instability, 
including elevated CAPE, is released by convergence/moist ascent
along the front and moist-isentropic ascent ahead of the 
shortwave trough axis. A SW'erly 30-40 knot LLJ should 
overspread our region ahead of the cold front overnight Saturday
night into Sunday and enhance the moist isentropic ascent. This
LLJ will slowly exit our region to the south and east Sunday 
night through early Monday afternoon as the cold front drifts 
SE'ward. Unusually-high PWAT's within the low-level warm/moist 
air advection regime from the Gulf and/or southern Gulf Stream 
should allow convection to produce periods of heavy rainfall. 
SW'erly mean mid-level flow should exhibit a large component 
parallel to the LLJ's major axis and cold front, and allow 
convection to train. Thus, localized flash flooding remains a 
concern. WPC still has WNY in a marginal risk of excessive 
rainfall (level 1 of 4) Saturday night and our entire CWA in a 
slight risk of excessive rainfall (level 2 of 4) Sunday into 
Sunday night. Additional and isolated showers and thunderstorms 
are possible on Monday, ahead of the shortwave trough axis and 
especially along and ahead of the surface cold front. Deep-layer
bulk shear strengthening to moderate to strong magnitudes may 
support stronger storms Saturday night through Sunday and into 
Monday, but the potential for stronger storms will be contingent
on multiple factors, including the magnitude of instability. 
Dry weather is expected to return region-wide by Monday night as
stabilizing subsidence accompanies the aforementioned ridge.

Lows should reach mainly the 60's overnight Saturday night.
Highs should reach the 70's Sunday afternoon. Lows should reach
mainly the mid 50's to mid 60's around daybreak Monday. Daytime
highs should reach the 70's on Monday and be followed by 
overnight lows in the lower 50's to lower 60's around daybreak 
Tuesday as a somewhat cooler and drier air mass overspreads our 
region behind the cold front.
